label: Def: CSC
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def: CSC}
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T})$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold.
Let $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ be a weight defined on the edges of $(M,\mathcal{T})$.
The combinatorial scalar curvature at a vertex $i\in V$ for Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric $r$ is defined as
\begin{equation*}                
K_i=\sum_{j;j\sim i}K_{ij}\cos \theta_{ij},
\end{equation*}
where $\theta_{ij}$ is the inner angle opposite to the edge with length $r_j$ in the hyperbolic triangle formed by three edges with lengths $r_i,\ r_j,\ l_{ij}$, as shown in Figure \ref{triangle}.
head: environment

label: Thm: local rigidity
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold with a weight $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfying (\ref{Eq: SC1}) or (\ref{Eq: SC2}).
If $\overline{r}$ is a non-degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric on $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ with $K_{ij}(\overline{r})\geq0$ for any edge $\{ij\}\in E$,
then there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $\overline{r}$ such that Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric in $U$ is determined by its combinatorial scalar curvature.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In the special case $\Phi\equiv 0$, the condition $K_{ij}(\overline{r})\sin^2\Phi_{ij}\geq0$ has no restrictions on the combinatorial Ricci curvature $K_{ij}$. In this case, Theorem \ref{Thm: local rigidity} reduces to the local rigidity of tangential hyperbolic sphere packings on 3-dimensional manifolds, a result claimed by Cooper-Rivin in \cite{CR}. In this paper, we give a rigorous proof of this fact as a by product of Theorem \ref{Thm: local rigidity}. The global rigidity of the tangential hyperbolic sphere packings has been proved in \cite{X1}.

title: Remark
body_md:
As mentioned in \cite{He-Xu}, there is a subtle difference between the notion of the local rigidity in Theorem \ref{Thm: local rigidity} and the infinitesimal rigidity in Theorem \ref{Thm: infinitesimal rigidity}.
In fact, the local rigidity implies the infinitesimal rigidity, but the reverse is not true due to dimensional differences.
head: environment

title: Conjecture
body_md:
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold with a weight $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$.
In the space of Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metrics on $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ with $K_{ij}(\overline{r})\sin^2\Phi_{ij}\geq0$ for any edge $\{ij\}\in E$, Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric is determined by the combinatorial scalar curvature.

label: Lem: none zero
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: Eq: F1
title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we assume $h_1\leq0$ and $h_2\leq0$.
By (\ref{Eq: h_i}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{Eq: F1}
\begin{aligned}
A_1\kappa_1
\geq&\ \kappa_2[x(1-w^2)+yvw+zuw+yu+zv]\\
    &+\kappa_3[y(1-v^2)+xvw+zuv+xu+zw]\\
    &+\kappa_4[z(1-u^2)+xuw+yuv+xv+yw],
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}\label{Eq: F2}
\begin{aligned}
A_2\kappa_2
\geq&\ \kappa_1[x(1-w^2)+yvw+zuw+yu+zv]\\
    &+\kappa_3[u(1-z^2)+xzw+yzv+xy+vw]\\
    &+\kappa_4[v(1-y^2)+xyw+yzu+xz+uw].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Hence, $A_1\geq 0$ and $A_2\geq 0$.
Moreover, multiplying the lefthand side of (\ref{Eq: F1}) with the lefthand side of (\ref{Eq: F2}) gives $A_1A_2\kappa_1\kappa_2$.
Multiplying the righthand side of (\ref{Eq: F1}) with the righthand side of (\ref{Eq: F2}) gives the sum of $\kappa_1\kappa_2[x(1-w^2)+yu+zv+yvw+zuw]^2$ and some nonnegative terms.
Thus
\begin{equation*}
Q_3:=A_1A_2-[x(1-w^2)+yvw+zuw+yu+zv]^2\geq0.
\end{equation*}
However, direct calculations give $Q_3=(1-w^2)Q_2$.
Lemma \ref{Lem: Q_2<0} shows that $Q_2\leq0$, and then $Q_3\leq0$.
Therefore, $Q_3\equiv0$, which implies $w=1$ or $Q_2=0$.

In the case of $w=1$,
since $Q_3\equiv0$,  the inequality (\ref{Eq: F1}) should be an equality, and the second and third terms in the righthand side of (\ref{Eq: F1}) vanish.
This implies $y=z=0$ and $x(u+v)=0$.
For (\ref{Eq: F2}), similar arguments yield $u=v=0$ and $x(y+z)=0$.
From the condition that the weight $\eta(E_\sigma)\in [0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$, we have $x\neq 1$.
Substituting $y=z=u=v=0$, $w=1$, and $x\neq1$ into (\ref{Eq: Q}) gives
\begin{equation*}
Q=(x^2-1)(\kappa_3+\kappa_4)^2<0.
\end{equation*}
By Lemma \ref{Lem: non-degenerate}, this contradicts the condition that $r$ is a degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric.

In the case of $Q_2=0$, Lemma \ref{Lem: Q_2<0} gives $A_i\leq 0$ for all $i\in\{1,2,3,4\}$.
By Lemma \ref{Lem: trivial}, this implies $Q\leq 0$.
From the condition $\eta(E_\sigma)\in [0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$, Lemma \ref{Lem: trivial} further yields $Q<0$.
By Lemma \ref{Lem: non-degenerate}, this contradicts the requirement that $r$ is a degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric.
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

label: Cor: one negative three positive

body_md:
\label{Cor: one negative three positive}
Suppose $(r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4)\in \mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$ is
a degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric on a tetrahedron with $\eta(E_\sigma)\in [0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$.
Then one of $h_1, h_2, h_3, h_4$ is negative and the others are positive.
head: environment

label: Thm: simply connect
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $r=(r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4)$ is a degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric.
Then by Corollary \ref{Cor: one negative three positive},
one of $h_1, h_2, h_3, h_4$ is negative and the others are positive.
Without loss of generality, assume $h_1<0$.
By (\ref{Eq: h_i}),
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\kappa_1A_1>&\ \kappa_2[x(1-w^2)+yvw+zuw+yu+zv]\\
    &+\kappa_3[y(1-v^2)+xvw+zuv+xu+zw]\\
    &+\kappa_4[z(1-u^2)+xuw+yuv+xv+yw]\geq 0,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
which implies that
$A_1=u^2+v^2+w^2+2uvw-1>0$.
In this case, take $Q\geq 0$ as a quadratic inequality $A_1\kappa_1^2+B_1\kappa_1+C_1\geq 0$ of $\kappa_1$,
where $B_1, C_1$ are given by (\ref{Eq: ABC}).
By Corollary \ref{Cor: positive Delta}, we have $\Delta_1=B_1^2-4A_1C_1>0$.
Therefore,
\begin{eqnarray*}
\kappa_1\geq\frac{-B_1+\sqrt{\Delta_1}}{2A_1}   \quad \text{or}  \quad
\kappa_1\leq\frac{-B_1-\sqrt{\Delta_1}}{2A_1}.
\end{eqnarray*}
The definition of $h_i$ in (\ref{Eq: h_i}) can imply $h_i=-\frac{1}{2}(2A_i\kappa_i+B_i)$.
Then $h_1<0$ is equivalent to $\kappa_1>-\frac{B_1}{2A_1}$.
Therefore,
$\kappa_1\geq\frac{-B_1+\sqrt{\Delta_1}}{2A_1}$,
which also implies $\kappa_1>\frac{-B_1}{2A_1}$ and $h_1<0$.

In the case where $A_1>0$, set
\begin{eqnarray*}
U_1=\{(r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4)\in \mathbb{R}^4_{>0}\mid \kappa_1\geq \frac{-B_1+\sqrt{\Delta_1}}{2A_1}\},
\end{eqnarray*}
which is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$ bounded by an analytic graph over $\mathbb{R}^3_{>0}$.
Similarly, we define $U_2, U_3, U_4$ whenever the corresponding $A_i>0$.
Note that $U_1,U_2,U_3,U_4$ are mutually disjoint by Lemma \ref{Lem: none zero}, if they are nonempty.

If $A_\mu>0$ for $\mu\in P\subset \{1,2,3,4\}$ and $A_\nu\leq 0$ for $\nu\in \{1,2,3,4\}\setminus P$, then the space of degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metrics
is $\cup_{\mu\in P}U_\mu$.
The corresponding admissible space of Thurston's sphere packing metric is
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\Omega_{1234}(\eta)=\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}\setminus\cup_{\mu\in P}U_\mu,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
which is nonempty.
Obviously, $\Omega_{1234}(\eta)$ is homotopy equivalent to $\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$, because
$U_1, U_2, U_3, U_4$ are mutually disjoint and bounded by analytic graphs on $\mathbb{R}^3_{>0}$.
This implies that, for any fixed weight $\eta$ with $\eta(E_\sigma)\in [0, 1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$,
the admissible space of Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metrics $\Omega_{1234}(\eta)$ is simply connected.  
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

title: Remark
body_md:
Condition (\ref{Eq: sum of Phi > pi}) in Corollary \ref{Cor: AS R4} includes the case $\Phi_{ij}\in [\frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{\pi}{2}]$.
Furthermore, (\ref{Eq: sum of Phi > pi}) permits some intersection angles to lie in $(0, \frac{\pi}{3})$.
Nevertheless, the configurations illustrated in Figure \ref{Figure: four circles} must be excluded.
Similar phenomena arise for circle packings with obtuse intersection angles \cite{Z}
and inversive distance circle packings with negative inversive distance \cite{X2} on surfaces.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The simply connectedness of the admissible space of tangential sphere packing metrics for a single tetrahedron was first proved by Cooper-Rivin \cite{CR}.
Xu \cite{X1} gave a different proof of the simply connectedness with an explicit description of the boundary of the admissible space.
Ge-Hua \cite{GH} gave some new viewpoints on the method in \cite{X1} for tangential sphere packings.
The proof of Theorem \ref{Thm: simply connect} for Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metrics unifies the proofs for simply connectedness in \cite{GH,X1}.
This method has been applied to give a new proof of the Bowers-Stephenson's conjecture for inversive distance circle packings on triangulated surfaces \cite{X3}, 
which simplifies the proofs of the Bowers-Stephenson's conjecture in \cite{Guo,L2,X2}.

label: Cor: connectness of 10-dim admissible space
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor: connectness of 10-dim admissible space}
The set $\Omega_{1234}$ is connected.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\eta_0\in W$.
By the nonemptiness of $\Omega_{1234}(\eta_0)$, there exists $r_0\in \Omega_{1234}(\eta_0)$ such that $Q(\eta_0, r_0)<0$.
Consider the continuous function $Q(\eta, r_0)$ in $\eta$.
Since $Q(\eta_0, r_0)<0$, there exists a connected neighborhood $U_{\eta_0}\subset W$ of $\eta_0$ satisfying $Q(\eta, r_0)<0$ for all $\eta\in U_{\eta_0}$.
By Theorem \ref{Thm: simply connect}, this implies that for every $\eta\in U_{\eta_0}$, any two points $(\eta, r_A)\in\Omega_{1234}$ and $(\eta_0, r_B)\in\Omega_{1234}$ can be joined by a path in $\Omega_{1234}$.
In this sense, the fibers $\Omega_{1234}(\eta)$ for $\eta\in U_{\eta_0}$ and $\Omega_{1234}(\eta_0)$ are path-connected within $U_{\eta_0}$.
Treating each fiber $\Omega_{1234}(\eta)$ as a single point,
we deduce that for any $\eta_A, \eta_B\in W=[0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$, there exists a path from $\Omega_{1234}(\eta_A)$ to $\Omega_{1234}(\eta_B)$ in $W$.
This follows from the connectedness of $W$ and the finite covering theorem, and it implies that $\Omega_{1234}$ is connected.
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

In \cite[Theorem 31]{Glickenstein JDG}, Glickenstein established a useful identity for the variations of dihedral angles in a Euclidean tetrahedron generated by 3-dimensional Euclidean discrete conformal structures. The identity \eqref{eq:C-diagonal} in Theorem \ref{thm C identity} is a hyperbolic version of Glickenstein's identity in the setting of Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packings.

label: Lem: matrix_negative
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Lem: matrix_negative}
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold with a weight $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfying 
$\eta(E_\sigma)\in[0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$ for any $\sigma\in T$ and $A_i\leq 0$ for any $i\in \sigma$ or the condition (\ref{Eq: SC2}).
The matrix $\Lambda=\sum_{\sigma\in T}\Lambda_\sigma$ is negative definite.
head: environment

label: Lem: 1
title: Lemma
head: environment
labels: eq: generalization of sum of angles

label: th-rank-one-det
title: Proof
body_md:
(a) By multilinearity in the columns,
\begin{equation}\label{th-rank-one-det}
\det M
=\det(P+\kappa\kappa^T)
=\det P+\sum_{t,p}\kappa_t\operatorname{adj}(P)_{tp}\kappa_p
=\det P+\kappa^T\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa.
\end{equation}
                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                
The identity $P\operatorname{adj}(P)=(\det P)I$ implies
\begin{align*}
M\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa
&=(P+\kappa\kappa^T)\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa\\
&=(\det P)\kappa+\kappa\bigl(\kappa^T\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa\bigr)\\
&=\bigl(\det P+\kappa^T\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa\bigr)\kappa\\
&=(\det M)\kappa,
\end{align*}
where \eqref{th-rank-one-det} is used in the last line.
As $M$ is invertible, this implies
\begin{equation}\label{th-h-adjugate}
h=M^{-1}\kappa=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa}{\det M}.
\end{equation}
                                                                
                                                                                                   
                                
     
                                     
                 
               
The $i$-th diagonal entry of $\operatorname{adj}(P)$ is
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ii}
=\det\begin{pmatrix}
-1&\eta_{jk}&\eta_{jl}\\
\eta_{jk}&-1&\eta_{kl}\\
\eta_{jl}&\eta_{kl}&-1
\end{pmatrix}
=\eta_{jk}^2+\eta_{jl}^2+\eta_{kl}^2
 +2\eta_{jk}\eta_{jl}\eta_{kl}-1.
\end{align*}
Under the hypotheses in (\ref{eq: generalization of sum of angles}), $\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ii}=A_i\le0$.
                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
               
             
                                                                                               
                                                                                          
                                                                                         
           
             
The off-diagonal entries of $\operatorname{adj}(P)$ are nonpositive.
In fact, if $i\ne j$ and $\{k,l\}=\sigma\setminus\{i,j\}$, then
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{aligned}
\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ij}=-\Big[&\eta_{ij}(1-\eta_{kl}^2)
 +\eta_{ik}\eta_{jl}\eta_{kl}
 +\eta_{il}\eta_{jk}\eta_{kl}
 +\eta_{ik}\eta_{jk}
 +\eta_{il}\eta_{jl}\Big]\leq 0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Since $\kappa_a>0$,
\[
(\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa)_i
=\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ii}\kappa_i+\sum_{j\ne i}\operatorname{adj}(P)_{ij}\kappa_j\leq0.
\]
Together with $\det M<0$ in (\ref{Eq: F26}), equation \eqref{th-h-adjugate}
therefore yields $h_i\geq0$.

(b) 
                                                     
                               
                                                     
   
                                       
                                                
                              
   
                                                                 
   
                     
                
                                                                          
                                                                          
                                                                        
               
   
                                               
                                                                                
By (\ref{Eq: F25}), we have
\begin{equation}\label{th-b-positive}
b_l^{(k)}=
\frac{\kappa_i(\eta_{ij}\eta_{jl}+\eta_{il})
+\kappa_j(\eta_{jl}+\eta_{ij}\eta_{il})
+\kappa_l(1-\eta_{ij}^2)}{\det M_{\{i,j,l\}}}.
\end{equation}
                                                                                                                                      
The denominator is positive, and the numerator are nonnegative. 
Thus $b_l^{(k)}\geq0$.
Moreover, $b_l^{(k)}=0$ if and only if $\eta_{ij}=1,
\eta_{il}=\eta_{jl}=0$.

(c) We first give the positive support of $h$.
Let
\[
I_+=\{i\in\sigma:h_i>0\}.
\]
Suppose that \(h_i=0\) for at least one \(i\).  Since
\((\operatorname{adj}(P)\kappa)_i\) is a sum of nonpositive terms with positive
coefficients \(\kappa_j\), the entire \(i\)-th row of \(\operatorname{adj}(P)\)
must vanish.  Therefore, \(\det P=0\).

On the other hand, $\det M<0$ in (\ref{Eq: F26}),  equation \eqref{th-rank-one-det}
therefore yields \(\operatorname{adj}(P)\ne0\).  
Hence $\operatorname{rank}P=3$. Note that $P\operatorname{adj}(P)=(\det P) I=0$, we have 
$\operatorname{rank}\operatorname{adj}(P)=1.$
Because \(\operatorname{adj}(P)\) is symmetric and entrywise nonpositive, there
exist \(\rho>0\) and a nonzero vector \(v\ge0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{adj}(P)=-\rho vv^T.
\]
The identity \(P\operatorname{adj}(P)=0\) yields \(Pv=0\).  Furthermore,
\[
\det M=-\rho(v^T\kappa)^2,
\qquad
h=\frac{v}{v^T\kappa}.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:support}
I_+=\operatorname{supp} v.
\end{equation}

The component form of \(Pv=0\) is $v_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\eta_{ij}v_j$.
If \(d\notin I_+\), then \(v_d=0\), and hence $0=\sum_{a\in I_+}\eta_{da}v_a$.
Since \(v_a>0\) and \(\eta_{da}\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crosszero}
\eta_{da}=0
\quad\text{for every }a\in I_+.
\end{equation}

The support \(I_+\) cannot be empty, because $h=\frac{v}{v^T\kappa}, v\geq 0$ and $v\neq 0$.
We further have that the support \(I_+\) cannot have only one element, because the corresponding
component of \(Pv=0\) would give \(-v_a=0\).  Therefore only the cases \(|I_+|=4,3,2\) are possible.

\noindent\textbf{Case 1: } Assume that $|I_+|=4$.

All \(h_i\) are positive.  
Suppose that $m_{kl}=0$. 
Then $b_l^{(k)}=b_k^{(l)}=0$.
Hence
\[
\eta_{ij}=1,\qquad
\eta_{ik}=\eta_{il}=\eta_{jk}=\eta_{jl}=0.
\]
If \(\eta_{kl}=1\), then \(\eta\in \widetilde{S}\), which is excluded.
If \(\eta_{kl}<1\), then, after a relabeling,
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&1&0&0\\
1&-1&0&0\\
0&0&-1&\eta_{kl}\\
0&0&\eta_{kl}&-1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its kernel is spanned by \(e_i+e_j\), so
\eqref{eq:support} would imply \(h_k=h_l=0\), a contradiction.
Thus \(m_{kl}>0\) for every edge.

\noindent\textbf{Case 2: } Assume that $|I_+|=3$.

Write $I_+=\{a,b,c\}$ and $h_d=0$.
Equation \eqref{eq:crosszero} gives $\eta_{ad}=\eta_{bd}=\eta_{cd}=0$.
For the edge \(\{a,d\}\), the complementary indices are \(b,c\).
Since \(\eta_{ad}=0\ne1\), it follows from (\ref{th-b-positive}) that $b_c^{(b)}>0$.
Since \(h_b>0\), $m_{bc}=h_b b_c^{(b)}+h_c b_b^{(c)}\ge h_b b_c^{(b)}>0$.
Similarly, $m_{ac}>0$ and $m_{ab}>0$.

\noindent\textbf{Case 3: } Assume that $|I_+|=2$.

Write $I_+=\{a,b\}$ and $h_c=h_d=0$.
The \(a\)- and \(b\)-components of \(Pv=0\) give $v_a=\eta_{ab}v_b$ and $v_b=\eta_{ab}v_a$.
Since \(v_a,v_b>0\), it follows that $\eta_{ab}=1$ and $v_a=v_b$.
The remaining components give $\eta_{ac}=\eta_{bc}
=\eta_{ad}=\eta_{bd}=0$.
For the cross edge \(\{a,c\}\), the complementary indices are
\(b,d\).  Since \(\eta_{ac}=0\), it follows from (\ref{th-b-positive}) that $b_d^{(b)}>0$.
Together with \(h_b>0\), this yields \(m_{bd}>0\).  Likewise, $m_{bc}>0$, $m_{ad}>0$, and $m_{ac}>0$.

(d) By Corollary \ref{Cor: AS R4}, under the condition (\ref{eq: generalization of sum of angles}), the admissible space is $\Omega_{1234}(\eta)=\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$.
By (\ref{eq:C-def}), to prove the negative definiteness of $\Lambda_\sigma$,
it suffices to prove that $C$ is positive definite.
For every $z\in \mathbb{R}^4$, we have
\begin{align*}
z^TCz
&=\sum_iC_{ii}z_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}z_iz_j\\
&=-\sum_i\sum_{j\ne i}C_{ij}\cosh l_{ij}\,z_i^2
  +2\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}z_iz_j\\
&=-\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}
\bigl[\cosh l_{ij}(z_i^2+z_j^2)-2z_iz_j\bigr]\\
&=-\sum_{i<j}C_{ij}
\left[(z_i-z_j)^2+(\cosh l_{ij}-1)(z_i^2+z_j^2)\right],
\end{align*}
where (\ref{eq:C-diagonal}) is used in the second line.

Lemma \ref{Lem: 1} (c) shows for any vertex $i$, there exists at least a vertex $j\sim i$, such that $b_l^{(k)}h_k+b_k^{(l)}h_l>0$.
Since $q>0$ and $E_{ij}>0$, it follows from (\ref{eq:Cij-basic}) that $C_{ij}<0$ for the edge $\{ij\}$.
Hence $z^TCz>0$ for any nonzero $z$.
This implies that $C$ is positive definite.
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

title: Proof
body_md:
Following the calculations in equation (\ref{eq A identity}) in the proof of Corollary \ref{Cor: AS R4}, we have $A_i<0$ under the condition (\ref{Eq: SC1}).
Furthermore, for any $\eta\in \widetilde{S}$, the corresponding intersection angles satisfy
$$\Phi_{ij}+\Phi_{jk}+\Phi_{ik}=\pi,\quad \forall\{ijk\}\in F_\sigma.$$
Therefore, under the condition (\ref{Eq: SC1}), $\eta(E_\sigma)\in[0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$.
By Corollary \ref{Cor: AS R4}, the admissible space is $\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$.
By Lemma \ref{Lem: 1} (d), the matrix $\Lambda_\sigma$ is negative definite for any $r\in\mathbb{R}^4_{>0}$.
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

label: Lem: 3
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: Thm: local rigidity2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm: local rigidity2}
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold with a weight $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfying 
$\eta(E_\sigma)\in[0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$ for any $\sigma\in T$ and $A_i\leq 0$ for any $i\in \sigma$ or the condition (\ref{Eq: SC2}).
If $\overline{r}$ is a non-degenerate Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric on $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ satisfying $K_{ij}(\overline{r})\sin^2\Phi_{ij}\geq0$ for any edge $\{ij\}\in E$,
then there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $\overline{r}$ such that Thurston's hyperbolic sphere packing metric in $U$ is determined by its combinatorial scalar curvature.

body_md:
\label{Thm: infinitesimal rigidity 2}
Suppose $(M,\mathcal{T},\Phi)$ is a triangulated connected closed 3-dimensional manifold with a weight $\Phi: E\rightarrow [0,\frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfying 
$\eta(E_\sigma)\in[0,1]^6\setminus \widetilde{S}$ for any $\sigma\in T$ and $A_i\leq 0$ for any $i\in \sigma$ or the condition (\ref{Eq: SC2}).
Then there exists a neighborhood $U\subseteq\Omega$ of $\overline{r}$ such that if $r\in U$ has the same combinatorial Ricci curvature as $\overline{r}$, then $r=\overline{r}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal{G}_{ii}=0$, $\det \mathcal{G}$ is a sum over $4$-point fixed-point-free permutations. 
Substitute (\ref{th-E}) and (\ref{Eq: F19}), 
expand exactly in the ring of integer polynomials $\mathbb{Z}[y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4,\eta]$, 
and perform polynomial division to obtain (\ref{Eq: F20}), with zero remainder.

For $0\le \eta<1$, introduce the nonnegative change of variables
\begin{equation}\label{73}
z=\frac{\eta}{1-\eta}\ge 0,\qquad \mathcal{Q}(y,z)=(1+z)^{10}\mathcal{P}\!\left(y,\frac{z}{1+z}\right). 
\end{equation}
With Wolfram Mathematica 12.0,  via exact integer expansion one can obtain all the  nonzero monomials in $\mathcal{Q}(y,z)$.  More precisely, to construct $\mathcal{G}$ in equation (\ref{Eq: F19}), one can run the following Mathematica code:

\bigskip

                          

$>$ $y = Array[yy, 4];$

$>$ $kap = y + 1;$

$>$ $vertices = Range[4];$

$>$ $edges = Subsets[vertices, \{2\}];$

$>$ $e[i_{-}, j_{-} ] := 
  kap[[i]]^2 + kap[[j]]^2 + 2*eta*kap[[i]] kap[[j]] + eta^2 - 1;$

$>$ $a[i_{-}, k_{-}, l_{-}\ ] := (kap[[k]] + 
     eta*kap[[i]])*(eta(kap[[i]] + kap[[k]]) + (1 - eta) kap[[l]]);$

$>$ $G = Table[
   If[i == j, 0, 
    With[\{rest = Complement[vertices, \{i, j\}]\}, 
     With[\{k = rest[[1]], $ $l = rest[[2]]\}, 
      e[i, j] (e[i, l]*a[i, k, l] + e[i, k]*a[i, l, k])]]], \{i, 
    4\}, \{j, 4\}];$
    
\bigskip

To  calculate the determinant of $\mathcal{G}$, we can run the following:


\bigskip

$>$ $derangements = 
  Select[Permutations[vertices], And @@ Thread[\# \neq vertices] \&]; $
  
$>$ $Length[derangements];$

$>$ $detG = Expand[
   Total[(Signature[\#] Times @@ Table[G[[i, \#[[i]]]], \{i, 4\}]) \& /@ 
     $ 
     
     $derangements]];$


\bigskip

To get  the polynomial $\mathcal{P}(y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4,\eta)$ in equation (\ref{Eq: F20}), we can run the following:


\bigskip

$>$ $divisor = Expand[(1 + eta)^2*Times @@ (e[\#[[1]], \#[[2]]] \& /@ edges)];$

$>$ $\{pPoly, remainder\} = PolynomialQuotientRemainder[-detG, divisor, eta];$

$
\{remainder === 0, Exponent[pPoly, eta]\}$


\bigskip

To obtain the  polynomial $\mathcal{Q}(y,z)$ in equation (\ref{73}), we can run the following


\bigskip

$>$ $degree = Exponent[pPoly, eta];$

$>$ $qPoly = Expand[
   Sum[Coefficient[pPoly, eta, j]*z^j (1 + z)^{(degree - j)}, \{j, 0, 
     degree\}]];$
     
                                                                                           

$>$ $Together[qPoly - (1 + z)^{10} (pPoly /. eta \rightarrow z/(1 + z))] === 0$


\bigskip

To verify the number of the nonzero monomials, the minimal coefficient 
of the nonzero monomials, the maximal coefficient of the nonzero 
monomials, the numbers of monomials with z-degree zero, and check all 
the coefficients are positive, we can run the following:


\bigskip

$>$ $rules = CoefficientRules[qPoly, Join[y, \{z\}]];$

$>$ $coefficients = Last /@ rules;$

$>$ $\{Length[rules], Min[coefficients], Max[coefficients], 
 Count[rules, rule_{-} /;$ 
 
 $ Last[First[rule]] == 0], 
 AllTrue[coefficients, Positive]\}$


\bigskip

To obtain all the coefficients of the nonzero monomials in $\mathcal{Q}(y,z)$, one can run the following:

\bigskip

$>$ $Q1 = qPoly /. \{yy[1]\rightarrow y1, yy[2] \rightarrow y2, yy[3] \rightarrow y3, yy[4] \rightarrow y4\};$

$>$ $Qnew = Expand[Q1];$

$>$ $vars = \{y1, y2, y3, y4, z\};$

$>$ $allRules = CoefficientRules[Qnew, vars];$

$>$ $coefficientTable = (Join[First[\#], \{Last[\#]\}] \&) /@ allRules;$

$>$ $coefficientTable = Reverse@SortBy[coefficientTable, Take[\#, 5] \&];$

$>$ $Export[FileNameJoin[\{NotebookDirectory[], ``Q_{-}coefficients.csv"\}], $

$
  Prepend[coefficientTable, \{``a1", ``a2", ``a3", ``a4", ``b", 
   ``coefficient"\}], ``CSV"]$

\bigskip

After running all the above codes, we find that $\mathcal{Q}$ has exactly $16160$ nonzero monomials, with all coefficients being positive integers; the minimal coefficient is $2$, maximal coefficient is $53861376$. 
There are $729$ terms with $z$-degree $0$, so even at $z=0$, $\mathcal{Q}(y,0)>0$. 
Hence $\mathcal{Q}(y,z)>0$ whenever $y_i>0,z\ge0$, which implies $\mathcal{P}(y,\eta)>0$. (The coefficients of all nonzero monomials of \(\mathcal{Q}(y,z)\) are provided in the attached file $\mbox{Q}_{-}\mbox{coefficients}$.csv.)

It remains to treat the endpoint $\eta=1$. For this purpose, we can run the following

\bigskip

$>$ $pPoly /. \{yy[1] \rightarrow y1, yy[2] \rightarrow y2, yy[3] \rightarrow y3, yy[4] \rightarrow y4, 
   eta \rightarrow 1\} // Simplify$
                                                                                     

\bigskip
The result is 
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{P}(y,1)=12\prod_{i<j}(y_i+y_j+2)^2=12\prod_{i<j}(\kappa_i+\kappa_j)^2>0. 
\end{equation*}
This proves (\ref{Eq: F21}).
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

body_md:
\label{Cor: rank=4}
Fix $\eta\in[0,1]$. 
Within the admissible space, $B$ is everywhere non-singular, 
and hence $Rank(\Lambda_\sigma)=4$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From (\ref{Eq: F22}) and Lemma \ref{Lem: 2},
\begin{equation*}
\det W = -\frac{(1+\eta)^2 \mathcal{P}(y,\eta)}{\prod_{i<j} E_{ij}} < 0.
\end{equation*}
By (\ref{Eq: F23}), $\det(U^T T)<0$. 
Together with \eqref{Eq: F15}, this yields $\det B>0$.
The conclusion follows from (\ref{eq:matrices}).
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove that $\Lambda_\sigma$ is negative definite for any $\sigma\in T$ and any $(\eta,r)\in \widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$, where
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma=\bigcup_{\eta\in\widetilde{W}}\big(\eta\times\Omega_{1234}(\eta)\big)=\big\{(\eta,r)\in\widetilde{W}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}^4\,\big|\,Q(\eta,r)>0\big\}
\end{equation*}
with
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{W}=\big\{\eta\in[0,1]^6\setminus S\,\big|\,\Phi\equiv C\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\big\}.
\end{equation*}
It is straightforward that $\widetilde{W}$ is connected, which implies $\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$ is connected by the similar proof of Corollary \ref{Cor: connectness of 10-dim admissible space}. 
It suffices to prove that the four eigenvalues of $\Lambda_\sigma$ are negative for any $\sigma\in T$ and any $(\eta,r)\in\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$.

For $\bar{\eta}=(0,0,0,0,0,0)$ and $\bar{r}=(1,1,1,1)$, we have $(\bar{\eta},\bar{r})\in\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$. 
In this case, all the intersection angles $\Phi_{ij}$ are $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
By Corollary \ref{Cor: negative under sum big than pi}, 
$\Lambda_\sigma(\bar{\eta},\bar{r})$ is negative definite.
By Corollary \ref{Cor: rank=4}, $Rank(\Lambda_\sigma(\eta,r))=4$ for any $(\eta,r)\in\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$. 
Combining the continuity of eigenvalues and the connectedness of $\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$, 
we have four eigenvalues of $\Lambda_\sigma$ are negative for any $(\eta,r)\in\widetilde{\Omega}_\sigma$. 
This implies the negative definiteness of the matrix $\Lambda_\sigma$.
\hfill{Q.E.D.}\smallskip
